topic: Why headline and core inflation figures tell different stories
setting: A live radio programme, Market Briefing, recorded on the morning of a major CPI data release; the tone is analytical and brisk, with the host pressing the guest on the policy implications of the diverging figures.

lines.speaker: HOST
lines.text: Welcome back to Market Briefing. Inflation figures released this morning show headline CPI has fallen to three point two per cent, yet core inflation remains stuck at four point six. Why the gap, and which number should we actually be trusting?

lines.speaker: ECONOMIST
lines.text: Well, that is the central tension right now, and it is not a new one. Headline CPI captures everything — food at the supermarket, petrol at the pump, energy bills — which makes it very visible to households. Core strips those out because food and energy prices move on global commodity cycles and seasonal factors that monetary policy simply cannot address in the short run. So when a central bank is calibrating interest rates, core gives a cleaner signal about domestic demand pressures.

lines.speaker: HOST
lines.text: But is that not a convenient distinction? Because for the majority of working families, food and energy are not optional extras that you can strip out of your weekly budget. Surely the gap between the two figures is doing real damage to public trust in official statistics.

lines.speaker: ECONOMIST
lines.text: I take that point, and I think it is a legitimate criticism of how we communicate these measures — not of the measures themselves. The Fed, the ECB, all the major central banks are quite transparent about why they focus on core. The problem is that the gap we are seeing right now — over one and a half percentage points — is unusually wide, and that is largely because energy prices have fallen sharply since last year's peak. So headline has dropped faster than underlying demand pressures have actually eased.

lines.speaker: HOST
lines.text: Which implies that core is telling a more cautious story than the headline figure would suggest?

lines.speaker: ECONOMIST
lines.text: Precisely. And that matters enormously for rate expectations. Markets saw this morning's headline print and immediately priced in two rate cuts by year end. I think that is premature. Core is telling you that services inflation, wages, domestic demand — the things a central bank can actually influence — are still running well above target.

lines.speaker: HOST
lines.text: So you are pushing back against the market consensus?

lines.speaker: ECONOMIST
lines.text: I am, yes. Not because markets are irrational, but because they are, I think, over-weighting a single data point. The trend in core needs to be sustained for at least two or three more months before you can confidently say that the tightening cycle is over.

questions.question: What does the economist imply about the market reaction to this morning's inflation data?

options.A: Markets have correctly concluded that the central bank's tightening cycle has run its course.
options.B: Markets should place greater weight on headline inflation than on core when forecasting rate decisions.
options.C: Markets are failing to recognise that energy prices have fallen since last year's peak.
options.D: Markets are drawing a policy conclusion that the available data does not yet support.

questions.rationale: The economist calls the market's two-cut pricing premature and says markets are over-weighting a single data point. He implies the data does not yet justify the conclusion that tightening is over.

option_rationales.A: Reversed relation: the economist says the tightening cycle cannot yet be called over and that the market view is premature.
option_rationales.B: Reversed: he argues central banks focus on core because it gives a cleaner signal, not headline.
option_rationales.C: Misattributed flaw: the economist himself explains the energy fall, and his objection is over-weighting a single data point, not ignorance of energy.
option_rationales.D: Correct: he says markets over-weight one print, and core needs two or three more months of sustained trend.

questions.question: How does the host regard the practice of excluding food and energy from the official inflation measure?

options.A: She implies it may serve the convenience of policymakers rather than reflecting the lived reality of most households.
options.B: She accepts it as the most reliable basis for central bank policy decisions.
options.C: She considers it methodologically sound but poorly explained to the general public.
options.D: She agrees with the economist's reasoning but argues it is being applied at the wrong moment in the cycle.

questions.rationale: The host asks whether the distinction is convenient and stresses that families cannot strip food and energy from their budgets. She implies the practice suits officials more than households.

option_rationales.A: Correct: her word 'convenient' and her point about family budgets imply it ignores lived reality.
option_rationales.B: Wrong speaker: the economist, not the host, argues core is the cleaner basis for policy.
option_rationales.C: Over-generous reading: she questions the distinction itself and never calls it methodologically sound.
option_rationales.D: Misread: she does not agree with his reasoning and raises no objection about timing in the cycle.

questions.question: When the economist concedes that the host's criticism is legitimate but directs it at communication rather than at the measure itself, what is he primarily doing?

options.A: Admitting that core inflation is a structurally flawed measure that central banks should revise.
options.B: Conceding that headline inflation is ultimately the more appropriate guide for interest rate decisions.
options.C: Suggesting that central banks have been deliberately withholding information from markets and households.
options.D: Acknowledging a valid concern about public transparency while defending the analytical rationale for core inflation.

questions.rationale: He grants the criticism of how the measures are communicated, but says it is not a criticism of the measures themselves. He then defends why central banks use core.

option_rationales.A: Overstates the concession: he explicitly says the criticism does not touch the measure itself.
option_rationales.B: Reversed: he continues to favour core for rate decisions and never concedes headline is the better guide.
option_rationales.C: Unsupported: he says central banks are quite transparent, so he rejects any suggestion of deliberate withholding.
option_rationales.D: Correct: he accepts the transparency concern but keeps defending core as analytically sound.
